sentence: A secondary dominant tonicizes a chord other than the tonic by borrowing the dominant of that target. In C major, the D major triad functions as V/V, resolving to G with its F-sharp acting as the leading tone of the dominant.

When analyzing V7/ii in a major key, expect the chordal seventh to fall by step into the third of the supertonic chord. The chromatic alteration raising the tone a half step below ii supplies the borrowed leading tone.

Secondary dominants frequently appear in chains, each one tonicizing the next: V7/vi to vi, reinterpreted as V7/ii, then to ii, then V7/V, V, and finally I. The sequence keeps every link a perfect fifth apart in root motion.

The applied dominant V/IV is identical in spelling to the tonic triad with an added minor seventh. Adding that flatted seventh transforms a stable C major triad into a C dominant seventh that pulls strongly toward F.

Voice leading into a secondary dominant demands care: the new chromatic pitch should usually enter by half step or be prepared as a common tone, avoiding an exposed augmented or diminished melodic interval in any single voice.

A secondary dominant of the minor subdominant introduces a chromatic pitch that anticipates the mixture to follow. The applied chord and the borrowed iv share the lowered submediant, smoothing the modal shift.

Identifying a secondary dominant requires checking whether a chromatically altered chord functions as the dominant of a non-tonic scale degree. If the suspect chord is a major triad or dominant seventh a fifth above its resolution, the analysis holds.

The resolution of V/V often deceptively moves to a cadential six-four rather than directly to the dominant triad. The bass still arrives on scale degree five, satisfying the applied dominant's pull while delaying the dominant proper.
In a minor key, V/III tonicizes the relative major. Because III is already a major triad, its applied dominant requires only the addition of a leading tone a half step below the mediant root.

A tonicized half cadence ends a phrase on a secondary dominant rather than the dominant itself, leaving the harmonic motion suspended one degree further from home and intensifying the expectation of continuation.

The Neapolitan sixth is a major triad built on the lowered second scale degree, conventionally voiced in first inversion so the fourth scale degree sits in the bass. In C minor it appears as D-flat major over F.

Resolving the Neapolitan, the lowered supertonic in an upper voice typically descends a diminished third to the leading tone, or moves through scale degree one as a passing tone, before the dominant arrives.

The Neapolitan most often functions as a chromatic predominant, substituting for the supertonic or subdominant. It progresses to the dominant, frequently through a cadential six-four that softens the augmented melodic leap.

Root-position Neapolitan chords occur in Romantic harmony, abandoning the conventional first inversion. Placed with the lowered second scale degree in the bass, the chord gains weight and the bass motion to the dominant becomes a striking diminished fourth.

Voice leading from a Neapolitan sixth to a root-position dominant produces a characteristic descent: the flatted second moves down to the leading tone, an interval of a diminished third that gives the progression its plaintive color.

Some analyses treat the Neapolitan as a chromatically altered supertonic, the flat-two being a lowered root of ii. Others read it as an independent predominant chord with its own functional identity in minor-mode harmony.

A tonicized Neapolitan is preceded by its own secondary dominant, the dominant of the flatted second degree. This applied chord briefly establishes the Neapolitan as a temporary tonic before the structural dominant reasserts itself.

The Neapolitan can be prolonged across several measures, harmonized with its own dominant and even passing six-three chords, before the structural progression continues toward the cadence on the home dominant.
Although most common in minor keys, the Neapolitan sixth also appears in major as a borrowed chromatic predominant. Its lowered second degree imports a touch of the parallel minor's darker coloring.

In four-part writing, the Neapolitan sixth typically doubles the bass note, which is the subdominant scale degree. Doubling the chromatic root would expose parallel motion problems when resolving to the dominant.

The Italian augmented sixth contains the interval of an augmented sixth between the lowered submediant in the bass and the raised subdominant above. Both pitches resolve outward by half step to an octave on the dominant.

A French augmented sixth adds the second scale degree to the Italian sixth, producing a chord with two whole-tone-related interval pairs. Its slightly dissonant inner sound distinguishes it from the German variant.

The German augmented sixth includes a perfect fifth above the bass, making it enharmonically identical to a dominant seventh chord. This equivalence enables smooth modulation by reinterpreting the chord as a true dominant elsewhere.

When a German augmented sixth resolves directly to the dominant triad, parallel fifths threaten between the bass and the chordal fifth. Composers often insert a cadential six-four to absorb the offending motion.

Augmented sixth chords function as intensified predominants. The augmented sixth interval expands to an octave on scale degree five, the two voices moving in contrary chromatic motion toward the dominant.
The enharmonic ambiguity of the German sixth permits a pivot modulation: spelled as a dominant seventh, it resolves down a fifth into a new key a half step away from the original tonic.
An augmented sixth chord built on the second scale degree, rather than the lowered sixth, tonicizes the dominant. This applied augmented sixth resolves to V as if V were a temporary tonic.
The rare English augmented sixth, a respelling of the French chord, places a doubly augmented fourth where the French has a perfect fourth, an enharmonic distinction with no audible consequence.

Augmented sixth chords most naturally arise from chromatic voice leading: a chord tone is pushed outward by half step in both directions, generating the characteristic interval that defines the sonority.

In minor keys the lowered submediant supplying the augmented sixth's bass is diatonic, so the chord requires only the chromatic raising of the fourth scale degree to complete its distinctive interval.

First species counterpoint sets one note against one note. Every vertical interval must be a consonance: perfect unisons, fifths, and octaves, or imperfect thirds and sixths, with no dissonance permitted anywhere in the exercise.

Parallel perfect fifths and parallel octaves are forbidden in first species because they collapse the independence of the two voices. Contrary or oblique motion into perfect consonances is strongly preferred.

A first species exercise begins and ends on a perfect consonance. The penultimate vertical interval is typically a major sixth expanding to an octave, or a minor third contracting to a unison, supplying the cadence.

Hidden or direct fifths and octaves, reached by similar motion in both voices, are avoided in first species, particularly when the upper voice leaps. The rule preserves the perceived separateness of the lines.

The counterpoint melody in first species should be primarily stepwise, with leaps used sparingly and balanced by stepwise motion in the opposite direction. A leap larger than a sixth is generally disallowed.

When writing first species above a cantus firmus, the climax of the counterpoint line should occur once and not coincide with the climax of the cantus, preserving the contour independence of the two voices.

Successive imperfect consonances of the same kind, such as a string of parallel thirds, are tolerated in first species but limited in number to prevent the voices from sounding like a single doubled line.
The unison is permitted only on the first and last notes of a first species exercise. Interior unisons momentarily fuse the voices and are therefore excluded from the strict discipline.

In first species the cantus firmus provides the fixed reference; every consonant choice in the added voice must also yield a singable melodic line, balancing vertical correctness against horizontal grace.

The melodic interval of an augmented fourth, the tritone, is banned in first species counterpoint melodies. The diminished fifth is likewise avoided, and any leap must be a consonant or stepwise interval.

Second species counterpoint places two notes against each one note of the cantus firmus. The downbeat must remain consonant, while the upbeat may carry a passing dissonance approached and left by step.

The passing tone is the characteristic dissonance of second species, occurring on the weak half of the measure. It fills the space between two consonances a third apart, moving stepwise in a single direction.
In second species, leaps from the strong beat to the weak beat are permitted only between consonances. A dissonant weak beat must always be a stepwise passing tone, never reached by a leap.
The first measure of a second species exercise often begins with a half rest, so the counterpoint enters on the weak half. This produces a momentary oblique motion against the held cantus tone.

Second species prohibits parallel perfect consonances on successive strong beats. Even when a weak-beat note intervenes, fifths or octaves landing on consecutive downbeats are heard as parallel and disallowed.
When the two notes of a second species measure outline the same harmony, the weak beat acts as a consonant skip rather than a passing tone, a permitted but melodically less smooth option.
The cadence in second species frequently uses the weak beat to introduce the leading tone, which then steps up to the tonic on the final downbeat against the cantus firmus.
A nota cambiata figure may appear in second species, a stylized melodic pattern in which a dissonant note is left by a leap of a third, an exception to the strict step-resolution rule.
Second species doubles the rhythmic activity of the added voice, so the contrapuntist must keep the melodic line shapely across twice as many notes while still observing strict dissonance treatment.
Direct fifths and octaves remain forbidden in second species. The intervening weak beat does not excuse similar motion into a perfect consonance on the following strong beat of the measure.

A suspension has three stages: preparation, where the note is a consonance; suspension, where the held note becomes a dissonance against a new bass; and resolution, where it steps down to a consonance.
The four-three suspension occurs over a root-position triad, the suspended fourth above the bass resolving downward to the third. It is among the most common ornamental dissonances in tonal harmony.
A seven-six suspension keeps a seventh above the bass on the strong beat, resolving down to a sixth. It is often chained, each resolution becoming the preparation for the next suspension.
The nine-eight suspension produces a momentary dissonant ninth above the bass that resolves to an octave. The suspended note must have been consonant in the immediately preceding chord.
A bass suspension, or two-three suspension, holds a dissonant note in the lowest voice. Unlike upper-voice suspensions, it resolves the dissonance by moving the bass itself down by step.
The retardation behaves like an inverted suspension: the held dissonant note resolves upward by step rather than downward. The leading tone retarded into the tonic is the most familiar instance.
A suspension may be ornamented before resolving, the suspended note decorated by a lower neighbor or an anticipation of the resolution pitch before finally settling onto the consonance.
Chains of suspensions create the characteristic gentle dissonance of sequential passages, each suspended voice resolving just as another voice prepares its own dissonance in the next link.
The change of bass suspension delays resolution by moving the bass to a new note that makes the held tone consonant again, postponing rather than canceling the dissonance.
Correct suspension writing requires that the resolution tone not sound simultaneously in another voice on the dissonant beat, a clash that would weaken the gentle effect of the delayed resolution.

The Dorian mode is a minor-type scale distinguished by its raised sixth degree. Compared with natural minor, that single chromatic difference gives Dorian its characteristically bright yet melancholy quality.

Phrygian mode features a lowered second scale degree, producing a half step at the very bottom of the scale. The descending half step from the second degree to the tonic gives Phrygian its dark color.
Lydian mode raises the fourth scale degree, replacing the perfect fourth of the major scale with an augmented fourth above the tonic. The result is a floating, unresolved brightness.

Mixolydian mode lowers the seventh scale degree relative to major. Without a leading tone, its dominant-to-tonic motion lacks the half-step pull, and the lowered seventh produces a flat-seven major chord.
Locrian mode has both a lowered second and a lowered fifth, making its tonic triad diminished. Because the tonic chord is unstable, Locrian is rarely used as a functional key center.
Each diatonic mode can be derived by starting the major scale on a different degree. Beginning on the second degree yields Dorian, on the third Phrygian, and on the fourth Lydian.

Modal harmony emphasizes the characteristic note that distinguishes a mode from its parallel major or minor. In Lydian, progressions that highlight the raised fourth confirm the modal identity to the ear.
The modes group into major-type and minor-type families. Ionian, Lydian, and Mixolydian have a major third above the tonic; Dorian, Phrygian, Aeolian, and Locrian have a minor third.
Avoiding the dominant-tonic cadence is essential to maintaining modal flavor, since functional dominant motion tends to pull the ear back toward conventional major or minor tonality.
A modal melody often circles around the characteristic degree and the final, the modal equivalent of the tonic, rather than progressing through tension and resolution as a tonal melody would.
The circle of fifths arranges the twelve pitch classes so that each step clockwise ascends by a perfect fifth. Adjacent keys differ by exactly one sharp or flat in their key signatures.
Moving clockwise around the circle of fifths adds sharps; moving counterclockwise adds flats. C major sits at the top with no accidentals, and the two directions meet enharmonically at the bottom.

Root motion descending by fifth, the strongest progression in tonal harmony, traces a counterclockwise path around the circle. The classic sequence vi-ii-V-I follows exactly this descending-fifth chain.
The circle of fifths predicts the closeness of key relationships. Keys adjacent on the circle share six of seven scale degrees and modulate to one another with minimal chromatic disturbance.
Relative major and minor keys share the same position on the circle of fifths because they share a key signature. The minor keys form an inner ring concentric with the major outer ring.
A complete circle-of-fifths sequence passes through all seven diatonic chords by descending fifths, though one link must be a diminished fifth to remain within the key without chromatic alteration.
Each major key signature can be read from the circle: counting positions clockwise from C gives the number of sharps, and counting counterclockwise gives the number of flats.
The interval of a perfect fifth, stacked twelve times, overshoots seven octaves by the small Pythagorean comma. Equal temperament shrinks each fifth slightly so the circle closes exactly.
Modulating to the dominant moves one step clockwise on the circle; modulating to the subdominant moves one step counterclockwise. Both are the closest possible key changes.
The circle of fifths also organizes the order in which sharps and flats appear in key signatures, sharps following the ascending-fifth sequence and flats following the descending one.

A perfect authentic cadence requires the dominant and tonic chords both in root position, with the tonic scale degree in the highest voice of the final chord. It produces the strongest sense of closure.
An imperfect authentic cadence weakens the closure of the full cadence: either a chord is inverted, or the soprano lands on the third or fifth of the tonic rather than the root.
The half cadence ends a phrase on the dominant chord, leaving the harmony open and unresolved. It demands a continuation, functioning as a comma rather than a period in the musical sentence.

A plagal cadence moves from the subdominant to the tonic, the so-called amen cadence. Lacking a leading tone, it confirms rather than establishes tonal closure, often appended after an authentic cadence.
The deceptive cadence sets up a dominant chord and then resolves it to a chord other than the expected tonic, most often the submediant. The thwarted expectation prolongs the musical phrase.
A Phrygian half cadence ends on the dominant approached by a first-inversion subdominant in minor, the bass descending a half step. The characteristic half-step bass motion gives it its name.
The cadential six-four delays the dominant by placing a tonic triad in second inversion on the strong beat. Its bass is the dominant scale degree, and the upper voices resolve down by step.
Evaded cadences occur when the expected resolution is interrupted by a sudden change of register, texture, or harmony, postponing closure and propelling the music forward into a new phrase.
The strength of a cadence depends on chord inversion, soprano position, metric placement, and harmonic rhythm. A root-position dominant-to-tonic on a strong beat with tonic in the soprano is maximal.
A Picardy third converts an expected minor tonic at a final cadence into a major triad by raising the third. The brightened final chord supplies a sense of resolved repose.
A time signature's upper number counts beats per measure and the lower number names the note value receiving one beat. Four-four meter therefore groups four quarter notes into each bar.

Simple meters divide each beat into two equal parts, while compound meters divide each beat into three. Six-eight is compound duple: two beats per measure, each a dotted quarter splitting into three eighths.
Asymmetrical meters such as five-eight or seven-eight group beats into unequal clusters. A seven-eight measure might be felt as a group of three plus a group of four, or any other partition.

The distinction between three-four and six-eight lies in beat grouping. Three-four has three beats each divided in two; six-eight has two beats each divided in three, despite both containing six eighth notes.
Duple, triple, and quadruple meters describe the number of beats per measure. Quadruple meter carries a secondary accent on the third beat, distinguishing it from a mere pairing of duple measures.
A pickup, or anacrusis, places one or more notes before the first full measure. The opening incomplete bar borrows its duration from the final measure so the total accounting balances.
Metric modulation reinterprets a note value across a tempo change so that a subdivision in the old tempo equals a beat in the new one, allowing a precise proportional shift in pulse.
Hypermeter extends metric organization beyond the bar, grouping measures themselves into strong and weak units. A four-bar hypermeasure treats its first downbeat as the strongest accent.
Polymeter superimposes two different meters simultaneously, one voice in three-four against another in four-four, the two cycles realigning only after their measures reach a common multiple.
The lower number of a time signature is always a power of two because Western notation builds note values by repeated halving, from the whole note down through eighths and sixteenths.

Sonata form unfolds in three large sections: an exposition presenting two contrasting key areas, a development that destabilizes the material, and a recapitulation that resolves the second theme into the tonic.

The exposition of a sonata movement establishes the tonic with a primary theme, then modulates through a transition to a secondary key, conventionally the dominant in major or the relative major in minor.
In the recapitulation, the second theme returns transposed so that it now sounds in the tonic. This tonal resolution, not thematic return alone, is the defining structural event of sonata form.

The development section freely fragments and recombines exposition material, modulating through distant keys and often building toward a retransition that prepares the return of the tonic on a sustained dominant.
A monothematic sonata exposition uses the same theme in both key areas, the contrast supplied entirely by the tonal shift rather than by a new melodic idea in the secondary key.
The medial caesura is a structural break, usually a half cadence with a rest, that divides the transition from the secondary theme and signals the arrival of the new key area.
A coda in sonata form extends the music past the structural cadence of the recapitulation, often revisiting developmental procedures and reinforcing the tonic with additional cadential confirmation.
Sonata-rondo form fuses rondo refrain logic with sonata tonal architecture: the first episode behaves like a sonata's secondary theme, returning in the tonic during the final refrain cycle.
The slow introduction preceding a sonata exposition often hints at thematic material in fragmented form and tonally prepares, sometimes obscures, the tonic before the fast exposition proper begins.
In minor-key sonata movements, the recapitulation may pose a tonal problem: the secondary theme originally in the relative major must be recast in the minor tonic, sometimes altering its character.

A fugue opens with a single voice stating the subject. The second voice enters with the answer, a transposition of the subject to the dominant, while the first voice continues with the countersubject.
A tonal answer adjusts certain intervals of the subject so that a leap to the dominant is answered by a leap to the tonic, preserving the key and avoiding premature modulation.
The exposition of a fugue is complete once every voice has stated the subject or answer. Episodes built from motivic fragments then connect successive entries throughout the rest of the piece.
Stretto compresses the time between subject entries so that a later voice begins the subject before an earlier voice has finished it, the overlapping statements intensifying the contrapuntal density.
Subject statements may be presented in augmentation, with doubled note values, or in diminution, with halved values, transforming the temporal scale of the theme without altering its pitch contour.

An invertible countersubject is composed so that it sounds correct both above and below the subject. Voices can exchange positions at the octave, tenth, or twelfth without producing forbidden intervals.

A fugal episode modulates between subject entries, typically sequencing fragments of the subject or countersubject. Episodes provide tonal motion and relief from the constant restatement of the theme.
The subject may appear in inversion, every ascending interval becoming a descending one of the same size, producing a mirror image of the original melodic line within the contrapuntal fabric.
A double fugue introduces two subjects, either successively or simultaneously. The two themes must be designed in invertible counterpoint so they can combine in either vertical arrangement.
A pedal point in the final entries of a fugue sustains the tonic or dominant in the bass while the upper voices complete their contrapuntal work, gathering the harmony toward the closing cadence.
In four-part chorale writing, the leading tone in an outer voice resolves up to the tonic. Doubling the leading tone is forbidden because both copies would then resolve, creating parallel octaves.
Common tones between successive chords should be retained in the same voice when possible, and remaining voices should move to the nearest available chord tone, minimizing total melodic motion.

The chordal seventh of a dominant seventh resolves downward by step. Failing to resolve it produces an unresolved dissonance, while resolving it upward creates a frowned-upon leap from a dissonant tone.
Parallel fifths and parallel octaves between any pair of the four voices are prohibited because they undermine the independence of the parts, momentarily collapsing two voices into one.
Voice crossing, where a lower voice rises above a higher one, is avoided in strict four-part writing. Overlapping, where a voice moves past where an adjacent voice just was, is similarly discouraged.
Spacing rules limit the gap between adjacent upper voices to an octave or less, while the tenor and bass may span a wider interval. Wide upper spacing thins the harmonic texture undesirably.
When a triad is in root position, doubling the root is the safest choice. The fifth may be doubled or omitted, but doubling the third of a major triad emphasizes a tendency tone unnecessarily.
A diminished triad in first inversion typically doubles the third, the bass note, because doubling the diminished fifth or the root would expose the unstable tritone in parallel motion.
Hidden octaves arise when the outer voices move in similar motion into a perfect octave with the soprano leaping. The rule guards against the aural impression of parallel perfect intervals.
When resolving a deceptive cadence from V to vi in major, the leading tone steps up to the tonic and the third of vi is doubled, an accepted exception to the usual root-doubling preference.
Figured bass notation places numerals beneath the bass line indicating the intervals to be sounded above it. A six signals first inversion, a six-four signals second inversion of a triad.
The absence of figures beneath a bass note implies a root-position triad, sounding a third and a fifth above the bass. The realization fills in the harmony according to voice-leading convention.
A seventh chord in root position is figured seven; in first inversion six-five; in second inversion four-three; and in third inversion four-two, each numeral set marking the intervals above the bass.
A sharp or flat standing alone in a figured bass applies to the third above the bass. An accidental beside a numeral chromatically alters the pitch at that interval above the bass note.
A slash or stroke through a figured-bass numeral indicates that the interval is raised a half step, a common shorthand for chromatic alteration in continuo realization.
Horizontal dashes after figures indicate that the harmony is sustained while the bass moves, the upper voices holding as the bass passes through nonharmonic tones beneath them.
Realizing a figured bass requires choosing voicing and doubling that satisfy the indicated intervals while producing smooth voice leading, the figures constraining harmony but not register.
The cadential six-four appears in figured bass as a six-four moving to a five-three over a stationary bass, the suspended fourth and sixth resolving down to the third and fifth of the dominant.
Figured bass economizes notation by specifying only intervals that depart from the default root-position triad, leaving the performer to supply conventional voicings for unfigured notes.
A consecutive series of first-inversion chords, figured with a row of sixes, produces a parallel six-three texture in which thirds and sixths above the bass move together.
A common-chord modulation pivots on a chord diatonic to both the old and new keys. The pivot is reinterpreted with a new Roman numeral, and a cadence in the destination key confirms the change.
Chromatic modulation alters a chord tone by half step to redirect the harmony, the chromatic voice leading itself accomplishing the shift without a chord shared by both keys.
An enharmonic modulation respells a chord so it functions differently in the new key. A German augmented sixth respelled as a dominant seventh permits a sudden move to a remote tonal region.
Phrase modulation, or direct modulation, simply begins a new phrase in a new key without any preparatory pivot, the change asserted abruptly at a structural seam in the music.
Modulation by sequence moves through a series of keys by repeating a harmonic pattern at successive transpositions, the sequence often abandoned once the desired destination key is reached.
A modulation to a closely related key requires only minimal chromatic adjustment, since adjacent keys on the circle of fifths differ by a single accidental and share most of their diatonic chords.
The common-tone modulation links two keys through a single shared pitch, the held note reinterpreted as belonging to a chord in the new key, often connecting chromatically distant tonal areas.
Tonicization differs from modulation in scale: a brief secondary dominant tonicizes a chord momentarily, while a true modulation establishes a new key with its own cadence and sustained presence.
A pivot-chord modulation between major and its relative minor exploits the fully shared key signature, making nearly every diatonic chord a potential pivot between the two tonal centers.
Modulation to the parallel minor or major involves a change of mode rather than of tonic, the shared tonic note allowing the new key to enter through chromatic mixture chords.
A passing tone fills the melodic gap between two harmony notes a third apart, moving stepwise in one direction. It is unaccented when it falls on a weak beat between consonances.
A neighbor tone steps away from a harmony note and returns to the same pitch. An upper neighbor rises and falls back; a lower neighbor descends and returns to its starting tone.
An appoggiatura is an accented nonharmonic tone approached by leap and resolved by step, the dissonance landing on a strong beat and creating a momentary expressive tension.
An escape tone steps away from a harmony note and then leaps in the opposite direction to the next chord tone, the reverse approach-and-departure pattern of an appoggiatura.
The anticipation sounds a chord tone of the next harmony before that harmony actually arrives, creating a brief dissonance against the current chord that resolves when the new chord catches up.
A pedal point sustains a single pitch, usually the tonic or dominant, while harmonies change above it. The held tone is consonant at the start and end but dissonant against the intervening chords.
A double neighbor figure surrounds a harmony tone with both its upper and lower neighbors before returning, the two embellishing tones forming a four-note ornamental pattern.
The accented passing tone falls on a strong beat, sounding dissonant against the prevailing harmony before resolving by step, distinguished from its unaccented counterpart by metric placement.
A changing tone, or cambiata, leaves a harmony note by step, leaps a third, and then steps back, a stylized melodic figure that treats its dissonance with a permitted leap.
Nonharmonic tones are classified by how they are approached and left: by step or by leap, and on a strong or weak beat. These two criteria distinguish every embellishing-tone category.
Roman numeral analysis labels each chord by its scale-degree root and quality. Uppercase numerals denote major triads, lowercase minor, a degree sign diminished, and a plus sign augmented.

In a major key the diatonic triads run I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, and vii diminished. The qualities are fixed by the scale: tonic, subdominant, and dominant are major; supertonic, mediant, and submediant minor.
Inversions are shown by appending figured-bass numerals to the Roman numeral. A first-inversion tonic in major appears as I with a six, indicating the third in the bass.
Functional analysis groups chords into tonic, predominant, and dominant categories. The supertonic and subdominant typically serve a predominant role, leading the progression toward the dominant.
A slash in Roman numeral notation indicates an applied chord: V over V means the dominant of the dominant, a secondary dominant tonicizing the fifth scale degree.
In minor keys the analysis must account for the variable sixth and seventh degrees. The raised leading tone produces a major dominant, while the natural minor seventh yields a flat-seven major chord.
Roman numeral analysis abstracts harmony from key, allowing the same progression to be recognized across transpositions. The numerals describe scale-degree function rather than absolute pitch.
A chromatic chord receives a numeral reflecting its altered root. The Neapolitan is labeled with a flat before a major-quality two, and augmented sixths get special symbols beyond ordinary numerals.
The cadential six-four is analyzed not as a tonic chord but as a dominant embellishment, often written as a dominant Roman numeral with six-four-to-five-three figures showing the resolution.
Prolongational analysis distinguishes structural chords from those that merely embellish or extend them, recognizing that not every labeled chord carries equal weight in the harmonic syntax.
The progression from tonic through predominant to dominant and back to tonic is the basic harmonic cycle of tonal music. Each function prepares the next in an expanding-then-resolving arc.
Root motion by descending fifth is the strongest progression in functional harmony. The chain ii to V to I exemplifies it, each chord falling a fifth into the next toward the cadence.
Retrogression describes a chord progression that moves against the conventional functional flow, such as a dominant proceeding back to a predominant, weakening the forward harmonic drive.
Harmonic rhythm refers to the rate at which chords change. A slow harmonic rhythm holds each chord for several beats, while a fast one changes harmony nearly every beat.
The lament bass is a stepwise descending bass line, often from tonic to dominant through chromatic passing tones, harmonized to support the characteristic falling melodic gesture above it.
A circle-of-fifths sequence chains chords whose roots descend by fifth, each link a transposition of the previous one, producing a smoothly modulating or tonally circling passage.
The phrase model organizes a typical tonal phrase into tonic prolongation, predominant arrival, dominant, and cadential tonic, a syntactic template underlying countless individual progressions.
Chromatic mediant relationships link chords whose roots lie a third apart and that share one common tone, producing a colorful, nonfunctional connection favored in Romantic harmony.
An auxiliary cadence is a progression that begins away from the tonic, on a predominant or dominant, and arrives at the tonic for the first time at the cadence itself.
Prolongation extends a single harmony across time through neighboring and passing chords, so that a long passage may be heard as one structural chord elaborated by subordinate motion.
Twelve-tone composition orders all twelve pitch classes into a row that is used as the basis of the piece. No pitch class repeats until the entire row has been stated.

The basic row generates three transformations: the inversion flips every interval, the retrograde reverses the order, and the retrograde inversion combines both, yielding forty-eight row forms with transposition.
A tone row can be partitioned into hexachords, tetrachords, or trichords. Combinatorial rows are constructed so that a row form and one of its transformations together complete the aggregate.

Transposing a twelve-tone row by an interval shifts every pitch class by the same amount. The interval content between successive notes, the row's defining feature, remains invariant under transposition.
The matrix is a twelve-by-twelve grid displaying all forty-eight forms of a row. Reading across gives transpositions of the prime form; reading down gives transpositions of the inversion.
Hexachordal combinatoriality occurs when the first six notes of one row form and the first six of another together exhaust all twelve pitch classes without duplication.
In strict twelve-tone practice, the row may be deployed melodically across a single voice or distributed vertically among chords, provided the ordering is preserved within each presentation.
An invariant is a pitch or interval pattern that survives a particular row transformation. Composers exploit invariants to create audible connections between otherwise contrasting row forms.
Integral serialism extends the ordering principle beyond pitch to organize duration, dynamics, and articulation by analogous numerical series, subjecting every parameter to systematic control.
The derived row is built by transposing and transforming a single trichord or tetrachord so that the segments together fill out all twelve pitch classes within one ordered statement.

Intervals are classified by quantity and quality. Quantity counts the staff positions spanned, while quality, ranging from diminished through perfect or major to augmented, fixes the precise distance.
The perfect intervals are the unison, fourth, fifth, and octave. They have no major or minor forms; shrinking or expanding them by a half step produces diminished or augmented intervals.

Inverting an interval within the octave changes its size so the two add to nine: a third inverts to a sixth, a fourth to a fifth. Major inverts to minor, augmented to diminished, perfect stays perfect.
Compound intervals exceed the octave. A ninth is a compound second, a tenth a compound third; reducing them by an octave reveals the simple interval that determines their harmonic quality.

Consonance and dissonance classify intervals by perceived stability. Perfect consonances are unisons, fifths, and octaves; imperfect consonances are thirds and sixths; seconds, sevenths, and the tritone are dissonant.
The tritone spans three whole tones and is the only interval that inverts to itself in size. Spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, it carries strong harmonic instability.

Enharmonic intervals sound identical but are spelled differently, like the augmented second and the minor third. Their notation reflects different functional contexts despite their equal-tempered equivalence.
The semitone is the smallest interval in twelve-tone equal temperament, dividing the octave into twelve equal steps. Two semitones make a whole tone, the basic step of the diatonic scale.
Interval class reduces an interval to the smaller of itself and its inversion, collapsing the twelve possible directed intervals into six undirected classes used in pitch-class set analysis.
A melodic interval sounds successively between two notes, while a harmonic interval sounds them simultaneously. The same interval can function differently depending on which dimension it occupies.
Schenkerian analysis reduces a tonal work to a fundamental structure: an upper-voice descent of the Urlinie supported by a bass arpeggiation through tonic, dominant, and tonic.
The middleground in Schenkerian theory occupies the level between the foreground surface and the background Ursatz, displaying prolongational events such as linear progressions and voice exchanges.
A linear progression connects two notes of a chord by passing motion through the intervening scale steps, the entire span heard as a prolongation of the harmony it spells out.

An interruption divides the fundamental line: the upper voice descends partway, reaches the dominant, and then restarts the descent from the initial tone, mirroring the structure of a parallel period.

Schenker's notion of structural levels treats surface detail as elaboration of deeper voice-leading frameworks, so an entire movement may be understood as a single elaborated tonic-dominant-tonic motion.
A voice exchange swaps two pitches between an upper and a lower voice across a span of music, prolonging a single harmony while creating contrapuntal motion between the exchanged tones.
The Kopfton, or head tone, is the first structural pitch of the fundamental line, the scale degree from which the Urlinie begins its descent toward the tonic.
Reaching-over is a voice-leading technique in which an inner voice is led above the main melodic line, momentarily taking over the upper part before the structural descent resumes.
An unfolding represents two voices of a polyphonic texture within a single notated line, the analysis revealing that one melodic strand actually carries two independent contrapuntal threads.
The bass arpeggiation, prolonging the tonic by passing through the dominant, supplies the harmonic foundation against which the fundamental upper-voice descent completes the Ursatz.
Jazz harmony routinely extends chords beyond the seventh to the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth. A major ninth chord stacks a major seventh and a major ninth above the root triad.

The eleventh is usually omitted or sharpened on a dominant chord because the natural eleventh clashes a half step against the major third. A sharp eleven supplies a lydian-flavored upper structure instead.
A dominant thirteenth chord contains the root, third, seventh, and thirteenth as its essential tones, the fifth and often the ninth dropped to keep the voicing lean and the guide tones prominent.
Altered dominants raise or lower the fifth and ninth, producing flat-nine, sharp-nine, flat-five, and sharp-five tensions. These alterations intensify the dominant's pull toward resolution.
An upper-structure triad voices a major or minor triad above the guide tones of a dominant seventh, the triad supplying a cluster of extensions and alterations heard as a bright chordal color.
Rootless voicings omit the chord root, leaving the bass to imply it. The pianist then voices the third, seventh, and chosen extensions, producing a transparent texture favored in ensemble playing.
A minor eleventh chord adds the ninth and eleventh to a minor seventh. Unlike on a dominant chord, the natural eleventh is consonant against the minor third and may be freely sounded.
Guide tones, the third and seventh of a chord, define its quality. Voicing them in smooth stepwise motion across a progression produces the connected lines characteristic of jazz comping.
A six-nine chord substitutes the sixth for the seventh and adds the ninth, creating a stable, non-functional sonority often used as a tonic resolution in jazz instead of a plain triad.
Tension and color tones are the ninths, elevenths, and thirteenths added above the basic seventh chord. Whether a tension is available depends on its half-step relationship to the chord tones.
Tonicization momentarily treats a chord other than the tonic as a local tonic by approaching it with its own dominant. The effect is brief, lasting only as long as the applied chord resolves.
A single secondary dominant tonicizes its target chord without establishing a new key. The ear registers a fleeting shift of tonal focus that is immediately reabsorbed into the prevailing key.
Tonicizing the subdominant requires lowering the seventh scale degree, since the dominant of IV needs a leading tone a half step below the fourth degree, which is the lowered seventh of the home key.
An applied leading-tone chord tonicizes its target just as an applied dominant does. A diminished seventh built on the leading tone of the target resolves to that chord as a temporary tonic.
The distinction between tonicization and modulation is one of duration and structural weight. Tonicization is local and transient; modulation establishes a new key with a confirming cadence.
Tonicizing the supertonic strengthens the predominant function. The applied dominant of ii sharpens the focus on the supertonic before the harmony continues through the dominant to the tonic.
A chain of tonicizations can carry the music through several local tonics in succession, each applied dominant resolving to a chord that is then itself tonicized by the next applied chord.
Extended tonicization prolongs a non-tonic chord with its own predominant and dominant over several measures, approaching the threshold of modulation without quite establishing the new key.
The tonicized half cadence ends a phrase on a tonicized dominant, the secondary dominant of V lending extra emphasis to the structural dominant on which the phrase comes to rest.
Tonicization within a sequence often passes through diminished or dominant seventh chords whose tonicizing function is local and decorative rather than structural, coloring the sequential motion.
Pitch-class set theory analyzes atonal music by grouping pitches into unordered sets. Each set is reduced to its normal form, the most compact ordering within an octave.
The prime form is the most compact and leftmost-packed representation of a set and its inversion, providing a label that identifies all transpositionally and inversionally related sets as one class.
An interval vector tallies the number of each interval class present in a set. The six-digit vector serves as a fingerprint of the set's intervallic content.
Transpositional equivalence treats two sets as the same if one maps onto the other by adding a constant to every pitch class. Inversional equivalence adds reflection to the set of allowed mappings.
A Z-related pair consists of two sets that share the same interval vector but are not related by transposition or inversion, an ambiguity that interval content alone cannot resolve.
Set classes are catalogued by cardinality and ordered within each size. The trichords, tetrachords, and larger collections each form a finite inventory of distinct prime forms.
The complement of a set contains all pitch classes the set omits. A set and its complement share closely related interval vectors, a relationship formalized by the hexachord theorem.
Computing normal form involves listing the pitch classes in ascending order, then rotating to find the arrangement spanning the smallest interval from first to last element.
Subset and superset relations describe how smaller sets embed within larger ones. Analyzing the recurring subsets of a piece reveals motivic coherence beneath an atonal surface.
The index number labels an inversion operation in pitch-class set theory. Inverting a set around a given index reflects each pitch class so the pairs sum to that constant value.
Syncopation displaces accent from the expected strong beat to a weak beat or an offbeat subdivision. The contradiction between notated meter and felt accent generates rhythmic tension.
A tie carrying a note across a barline so that it sounds through the following downbeat produces syncopation by suppressing the metric accent that would normally fall there.
Hemiola superimposes a triple grouping on duple meter or a duple grouping on triple meter. Three groups of two replace two groups of three within the same total duration.
Cross-rhythm sets two conflicting pulse divisions against each other simultaneously, such as three evenly spaced notes in one voice against four in another over the same span.
An offbeat accent stresses the subdivision between beats rather than the beats themselves. Sustained offbeat emphasis can momentarily reorient the listener's sense of where the downbeat lies.
Augmentation lengthens every note value of a rhythmic figure by a constant proportion, while diminution shortens them, transforming the temporal scale of a motive without altering its proportions.
A rhythmic ostinato repeats a fixed pattern persistently, establishing a steady reference against which other voices may introduce syncopation, hemiola, or cross-rhythmic conflict.
Anticipatory syncopation sounds a note slightly before its expected metric position, the early arrival creating a forward lean that propels the rhythm into the next beat.
Additive rhythm builds longer durations by summing small irregular units, grouping a stream of equal pulses into clusters of unequal length such as three plus three plus two.
Polyrhythm layers independent rhythmic cycles that realign only after a number of beats equal to the least common multiple of their lengths, producing a slowly shifting composite pattern.
The major scale follows the interval pattern of whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. This sequence of steps placed on any starting pitch produces a major scale in that key.
The natural minor scale uses the pattern whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. It shares its pitch collection with the relative major scale beginning a minor third higher.
The harmonic minor scale raises the seventh degree of natural minor, creating an augmented second between the sixth and seventh degrees and supplying a leading tone for a major dominant.
The melodic minor scale raises both the sixth and seventh degrees when ascending, smoothing the augmented second, and conventionally reverts to natural minor when descending.
A pentatonic scale contains five pitches per octave. The major pentatonic omits the fourth and seventh degrees of the major scale, removing the half steps and the tritone.
The whole-tone scale divides the octave into six equal whole steps. Lacking half steps and perfect fifths, it produces a symmetrical, tonally ambiguous collection.
The octatonic scale alternates whole and half steps, yielding eight pitches per octave. Its symmetry under transposition by a minor third gives only three distinct octatonic collections.
The chromatic scale comprises all twelve pitches a half step apart. As a complete collection it has no internal hierarchy, every pitch class equally available.
Synthetic scales are constructed by deliberately choosing an interval pattern outside the standard diatonic and minor forms, composers inventing collections to suit a particular harmonic vocabulary.
The blues scale adds a chromatic flatted fifth, the blue note, to the minor pentatonic, the added pitch sliding expressively between the fourth and fifth scale degrees.
Monophonic texture consists of a single melodic line without accompaniment. Even when many performers sound the line in unison or octaves, the texture remains monophonic.
Homophonic texture presents one prominent melody supported by subordinate harmony. The accompanying voices move primarily to support the tune rather than to assert independent melodic interest.
Polyphonic texture weaves two or more independent melodic lines simultaneously. Each voice carries its own contour and rhythmic profile, the lines combining into a coherent contrapuntal whole.
Heterophony arises when multiple voices perform variants of the same melody at once, the simultaneous embellished versions producing a loosely related cluster of melodic strands.
Homorhythmic texture, a subtype of homophony, moves all voices in the same rhythm. The chorale style exemplifies it, every part articulating each chord together.
Melody with accompaniment is the most common homophonic arrangement, a single foreground tune set against a chordal or figurated background that fills out the harmony.
Contrapuntal density measures how many independent voices are active at once. A texture may thicken as voices enter in imitation and thin as they drop out.
Imitative polyphony introduces a melodic idea in one voice and then echoes it in others at staggered entries, the overlapping statements producing the characteristic woven texture of a fugue.
Antiphonal texture alternates two contrasting groups, each answering the other in dialogue. The spatial and timbral separation of the groups structures the music into call and response.
Textural change is itself a formal device: a sudden shift from dense polyphony to sparse monophony, or the reverse, can articulate a structural boundary as clearly as a cadence.
The fully diminished seventh chord stacks three minor thirds, dividing the octave into four equal parts. Its symmetry means every inversion sounds identical in interval content.
Because the diminished seventh is symmetrical, any of its four notes can function as the leading tone. Each enharmonic respelling resolves the chord into a different key.
A half-diminished seventh chord, also called a minor seventh flat five, combines a diminished triad with a minor seventh. It commonly serves as the supertonic seventh in minor keys.
The leading-tone diminished seventh resolves to the tonic, each of its tendency tones moving by half step or step into a chord member of the resolving harmony.
An applied diminished seventh tonicizes a target chord, built on the leading tone of that chord. Its resolution behaves exactly like a leading-tone seventh resolving to a local tonic.
The common-tone diminished seventh shares a pitch with the chord it embellishes and resolves outward by half steps, decorating a triad rather than functioning as a true dominant substitute.
Resolving a fully diminished seventh, the chordal seventh and the diminished fifth both descend while the root and third ascend, the four voices converging by half step onto the resolution.
Enharmonic reinterpretation of a diminished seventh exploits its symmetry: respelling one tone as a leading tone of a distant key permits an abrupt and economical modulation.
Three distinct fully diminished seventh chords exist, since the symmetrical structure repeats every minor third. Each contains four pitches, and together they exhaust all twelve pitch classes.
The half-diminished seventh lacks the symmetry of the fully diminished chord. Its inversions sound different, and it functions as a colored predominant rather than a freely modulating pivot.
A cantus firmus is a given melody, usually in whole notes, against which counterpoint is composed. In strict species exercises it provides the fixed line that constrains the added voice.
A well-constructed cantus firmus moves predominantly by step, contains a single clear melodic climax, and spans a range no wider than a tenth, balancing motion against repose.
The cantus firmus begins and ends on the modal final. Its penultimate note is typically the second degree above or the leading tone below, stepping into the final at the close.
Leaps within a cantus firmus are limited in size and number. A leap larger than a third is balanced by stepwise motion in the opposite direction to recover melodic equilibrium.
A cantus firmus avoids repeating the same pitch consecutively and avoids outlining dissonant intervals such as the tritone across two leaps, keeping the line smoothly singable.
The climax of a cantus firmus, its highest note, should occur exactly once and be placed asymmetrically rather than at the midpoint, giving the melody a sense of direction.
Historically the cantus firmus was often a borrowed plainchant melody, set in long note values while newly composed voices elaborated counterpoint around the slow-moving foundation.
In cantus firmus mass composition, a single melody recurs as the structural backbone of every movement, unifying the cycle while the surrounding voices vary from movement to movement.
A paraphrase technique ornaments a borrowed cantus firmus, breaking its long notes into more active rhythmic figures so the foundation melody migrates into the texture rather than standing apart.
The cantus firmus may be placed in any voice of a contrapuntal texture. Setting it in the bass, tenor, or soprano changes how the surrounding counterpoint must be designed.
A chord is in root position when its root is the lowest sounding note. Placing the third in the bass produces first inversion, and placing the fifth in the bass produces second inversion.
First-inversion triads have a lighter, less stable quality than root-position triads. A passage of consecutive first-inversion chords produces a smooth, gently mobile harmonic texture.
Second-inversion triads are unstable because the bass forms a dissonant fourth with the root. Their use is restricted to specific contexts: cadential, passing, pedal, and arpeggiated six-fours.
The cadential six-four is a tonic triad in second inversion that ornaments the dominant. Its dissonant fourth and sixth above the bass resolve down to the third and fifth.
A passing six-four chord harmonizes a stepwise passing tone in the bass, connecting two positions of the same harmony with a momentary second-inversion chord on the weak beat.
A pedal six-four embellishes a static harmony: the bass holds while upper voices move up and back, momentarily forming a six-four chord before returning to the original position.
Seventh chords have four positions: root position and three inversions, each placing a different chord member in the bass and named by the figured-bass intervals it produces.
The bass note of an inverted chord determines its figured-bass symbol and its voice-leading behavior, since the lowest voice carries special weight in defining harmonic stability.
An arpeggiated six-four results when the bass arpeggiates through the chord tones, momentarily reaching the fifth in the bass without the six-four functioning as an independent harmony.
Inverting a chord redistributes its tones but preserves its harmonic identity and root. The root, not the bass note, remains the basis for Roman numeral analysis of the chord.
A ground bass is a short repeating bass pattern over which the upper voices spin continuous variations. The fixed foundation grounds the harmony while the surface above it is constantly renewed.
The passacaglia builds variations over an ostinato bass, typically in triple meter and a minor key. Each repetition of the bass supports a new contrapuntal or figurative treatment above.
A chaconne varies a repeating harmonic progression rather than strictly a bass line, allowing the bass itself to be embellished while the underlying chord sequence recurs.
Theme and variations form states a melody plainly, then presents successive transformations that vary its rhythm, harmony, mode, texture, or figuration while preserving its underlying structure.
A character variation reimagines the theme in a contrasting style or mood, recasting it as a march, a minuet, or a slow lament while keeping its phrase structure recognizable.
Double variations alternate between two themes, varying each in turn. The form derives contrast from the interplay of the two melodic sources across successive variation pairs.
In a variation set, the harmonic skeleton of the theme often remains constant even as the surface melody dissolves into rapid figuration, the chord progression anchoring the listener.
A cantus firmus variation places the unchanged theme in one voice as a fixed line while the other voices supply progressively elaborate counterpoint around it.
The figural variation maintains the theme's harmony and phrase lengths but replaces its melody with a consistent rhythmic or arpeggiated pattern, the same figuration applied throughout.
A final variation in a set often expands in length and intensity, sometimes incorporating a fugato or a coda that gathers the work toward a decisive conclusion.
A period consists of two phrases, an antecedent ending with a weak cadence and a consequent ending with a stronger one. The consequent answers and resolves the question posed by the antecedent.
A parallel period begins both phrases with the same melodic material, the contrast supplied by their differing cadences rather than by new thematic content in the consequent.
A contrasting period opens its consequent phrase with material distinct from the antecedent, the two phrases linked by the antecedent-weak, consequent-strong cadential relationship.
The sentence is a phrase type built from a two-bar basic idea, its repetition, and a continuation that fragments the idea and accelerates toward the cadence.
Phrase expansion lengthens a phrase beyond its expected norm through internal repetition, sequence, or cadential evasion, stretching the standard four- or eight-bar unit.
A double period groups four phrases, the first three ending with weaker cadences and the fourth with the strongest, the larger structure echoing the antecedent-consequent logic at a higher level.
Phrase elision occurs when the final note of one phrase simultaneously serves as the first note of the next, the overlap compressing the seam between consecutive units.
A presentation phrase establishes a basic idea and repeats it, often over a tonic prolongation, before the continuation phrase begins the harmonic and rhythmic acceleration.
Cadential strength orders the closural force of phrase endings: a perfect authentic cadence is stronger than an imperfect one, which in turn outranks a half cadence.
Phrase rhythm describes the pattern of phrase lengths and their cadential punctuation across a passage, the grouping of phrases shaping the listener's sense of musical syntax.
Quartal harmony builds chords by stacking fourths rather than thirds. A three-note quartal chord spans two perfect fourths, producing an open, ambiguous sonority distinct from triadic harmony.
Because quartal chords lack the third that defines major or minor quality, they sound tonally neutral. Their suspended, unresolved character suits impressionist and modal jazz contexts.
A stack of perfect fourths can be inverted to reveal a chord built of fifths, the two arrangements sharing the same pitch content viewed from opposite ends.
Quintal harmony, the close cousin of quartal harmony, stacks perfect fifths. The wide, hollow spacing of fifth-built chords evokes an archaic, open resonance.
Mixing perfect and augmented fourths in a quartal stack introduces a tritone, sharpening the otherwise mild dissonance of the chord and lending it a more pungent color.
Quartal voicings are common in modal jazz piano, where a fourth-based left-hand chord supports improvisation over a static mode without committing to functional major or minor harmony.
A quartal melody outlines successive fourths, the angular contour contrasting with the smoother stepwise and triadic motion of traditional tonal melody.
Parallel quartal chords gliding in similar motion produce planing, a texture in which the chord shape is preserved while the whole structure slides along the scale.
Quartal harmony resists conventional voice-leading rules because its constituent fourths do not form the tendency-tone relationships that govern triadic resolution.
Combining quartal and tertian structures, a composer may stack fourths above a triadic root, the hybrid chord blending functional grounding with the floating quality of fourth-built upper voices.
Transposition shifts every pitch of a passage by the same interval, preserving the internal interval structure. The transposed music sounds in a new key but retains its melodic and harmonic shape.
Transposing a melody up a perfect fifth raises each note by seven semitones. The relative distances between notes are unchanged, so the tune remains recognizably itself in the new register.
A transposing instrument sounds at a pitch different from its written note. A B-flat clarinet's written C sounds a B-flat, so its part is notated a whole step above concert pitch.
Modulation can be understood as a transposition applied locally, the music shifting to a new tonal center while the diatonic relationships within the new key mirror those of the old.
Transposing by interval class is the basic operation of pitch-class set theory, adding a constant modulo twelve to every pitch class and mapping a set onto a transpositionally equivalent set.
A sequence is a transposed repetition of a melodic or harmonic unit, each successive statement shifted by the same interval, the pattern propelling the music through changing pitch levels.
Transposing a chord progression preserves every Roman numeral, since the numerals describe scale-degree function independent of absolute pitch, only the key signature changing.
Chromatic transposition by a non-diatonic interval can carry music into a remote key, while diatonic transposition shifts within a scale and may alter chord qualities along the way.
Real transposition moves every interval exactly, while tonal transposition adjusts intervals to stay within a key, the latter sometimes changing major thirds to minor as the pattern shifts degree.
An octave transposition shifts pitches by twelve semitones, leaving pitch class unchanged. Such a shift alters register and timbre without affecting harmonic function.
Modal mixture borrows chords from the parallel mode, importing the minor subdominant or the lowered submediant into a major key for a darker harmonic color.
The borrowed minor iv in a major key lowers the sixth scale degree. The chromatic descent of that lowered tone to the dominant gives the progression a poignant inflection.
A flatted-six major triad, the lowered submediant borrowed from the parallel minor, often functions as a chromatic predominant or as the goal of a deceptive resolution in a major key.
The borrowed minor tonic in a major-key passage darkens the home harmony, the lowered third introducing the parallel minor's coloring without a full change of mode.
Mixture chords frequently cluster around the predominant function, the borrowed subdominant-area harmonies preparing the dominant with imported chromatic pitches from the parallel minor.
The flatted-seven major triad, borrowed from the parallel minor or the Mixolydian mode, supplies a nonfunctional, plagal-flavored harmony common in rock and folk-influenced music.
A major-key cadence may borrow the minor mode's flatted submediant for a deceptive resolution, the dominant resolving to the lowered-six major triad instead of the expected submediant minor.
Mode mixture can also work in reverse, a minor-key passage borrowing the brighter major-mode subdominant or the raised submediant for a momentary lift toward the parallel major.
The Picardy third is a form of mixture, the final tonic of a minor-key piece borrowing the major third of the parallel major to brighten the closing chord.
Chromatic mixture chords retain their original scale-degree function, so a borrowed minor iv still acts as a subdominant despite the lowered tone imported from the parallel mode.
A trill rapidly alternates the written note with the diatonic note above it. In Baroque practice the trill usually begins on the upper auxiliary, the dissonance resolving onto the main note.
The mordent oscillates quickly between the written note and the note immediately below it before settling on the principal pitch, a brief flick of decoration on a single tone.
An appoggiatura ornament leans onto the beat with a dissonant note that takes part of the principal note's value before resolving downward by step to the harmony tone.
A turn weaves around the principal note, touching the upper neighbor, the note itself, the lower neighbor, and the note again, a four-note figure that gracefully decorates a sustained pitch.
The acciaccatura, or crushed grace note, is played as quickly as possible just before the principal note, its written value notionally subtracted from nothing rather than from the main note.
Ornamentation in Baroque music is partly improvised, performers adding trills, turns, and passing figures to a sparse notated line according to the conventions of the style.
A division divides a long note into a flurry of shorter ones, a Renaissance and Baroque practice of melodic embellishment that elaborates a simple skeleton into virtuosic figuration.
The slide ornament approaches the principal note by a quick ascending step or two, the auxiliary notes leading smoothly into the structural tone on the beat.
A grace note is a small printed note with no nominal duration in the meter, borrowing its time from an adjacent note to add a brief decorative inflection.
Realizing ornaments correctly depends on period and national style, since the same sign denoted different figures in French, Italian, and German practice across the Baroque era.
Harmonic rhythm is the rate at which the underlying harmony changes, independent of the surface rhythmic activity. A passage may bustle with fast notes over a single slowly changing chord.
Accelerating harmonic rhythm toward a cadence intensifies the drive to closure, the chords changing more frequently as the phrase approaches its goal.
A slow harmonic rhythm at the opening of a movement allows a theme to unfold over stable harmony, while a quickening of chord change later signals structural intensification.
Harmonic rhythm and metric accent often align, with chord changes falling on strong beats. A chord change on a weak beat can produce a subtle syncopation of the harmony itself.
The relationship between surface rhythm and harmonic rhythm shapes textural energy: rapid figuration over static harmony feels decorative, while frequent chord change feels structurally active.
A pedal point freezes harmonic rhythm in the bass even as upper voices change chords above it, the sustained tone holding the harmony stationary at one structural level.
Sequences typically maintain a steady harmonic rhythm, each transposed link occupying the same span, the regularity reinforcing the sense of patterned motion.
Doubling the harmonic rhythm, changing chords twice as often, can mark the arrival of a developmental or transitional passage where harmonic instability increases.
Harmonic rhythm interacts with phrase structure: a cadence usually coincides with a return to slower chord change, the harmony settling as the phrase comes to rest.
The perceived tempo of a piece depends partly on harmonic rhythm, since rapid chord change can make a moderate surface tempo feel urgent and driven.
A cadenza is an extended solo passage, often improvisatory in character, inserted near the end of a concerto movement after the orchestra arrives on a cadential six-four.
The harmonic frame of a classical cadenza begins on the dominant prepared by a six-four chord and ends on a trill over the dominant, cueing the orchestra to re-enter for the final tonic.
A cadenza typically revisits the movement's principal themes, fragmenting and recombining them in free figuration before resolving the suspended dominant harmony.
Although improvised in earlier practice, cadenzas were later written out by composers, fixing the soloist's elaboration within the score rather than leaving it to spontaneous invention.
The structural function of the cadenza is to prolong the dominant, the soloist's display delaying the resolution to the tonic that completes the movement's harmonic motion.
A cadenza may modulate freely through distant keys, exploiting its position outside the strict harmonic syntax to explore tonal regions before returning to the home dominant.
The closing trill of a cadenza, sustained over the dominant, signals the impending orchestral re-entry, the trill resolving as the full ensemble arrives on the tonic.
An accompanied cadenza integrates orchestral participation, the soloist's elaboration unfolding against held chords or motivic interjections rather than in complete solitude.
Cadenzas appear not only in concertos but in arias and instrumental fantasias, wherever the form permits an extended, harmonically suspended display of the performer's invention.
The eingang, a shorter lead-in, performs a related function on a smaller scale, a brief solo flourish that connects two sections over a prolonged dominant.
Consonance and dissonance describe the relative stability of intervals and chords. Consonances sound stable and at rest; dissonances create tension that seeks resolution to a consonance.
The historical treatment of dissonance is strict: a dissonant interval must be prepared, sounded, and resolved according to convention, never left exposed or approached carelessly.
The perfect fourth is a context-dependent interval, consonant between upper voices but dissonant when formed against the bass, where it requires resolution like other dissonances.
Dissonance treatment defines compositional style: strict counterpoint permits dissonance only as carefully controlled passing tones, neighbors, and suspensions on prescribed beats.
The emancipation of dissonance, a twentieth-century development, abandoned the requirement that dissonant sonorities resolve, treating them as stable structures in their own right.
A dissonance's tension depends on context and register. The same interval may sound mild in a thick texture and harsh when exposed between two clearly heard voices.
Resolution converts dissonance to consonance by stepwise motion, the unstable tone typically moving down or up a step into a chord member of a consonant sonority.
Functional dissonance, such as the seventh of a dominant chord, carries harmonic meaning, its resolution participating in the syntax of the progression rather than merely ornamenting it.
Sensory consonance, rooted in the acoustics of overlapping overtones, partly explains why simple frequency ratios sound smoother than complex ones to most listeners.
The gradual historical expansion of accepted dissonance, from thirds in early polyphony to unresolved seventh and ninth chords later, traces the loosening of contrapuntal constraint.
An ostinato is a persistently repeated musical figure, melodic or rhythmic, that recurs unchanged while other elements vary above or around it.
A pedal point sustains a single pitch in one voice while harmonies shift around it. The held tone is consonant with the surrounding chords at its onset and resolution but dissonant between.
A tonic pedal anchors a passage on the home pitch, often at the opening of a movement, the sustained tonic grounding the harmony even as upper voices introduce passing chromaticism.
A dominant pedal builds tension by holding the fifth scale degree beneath changing harmony, the sustained dominant intensifying the expectation of an eventual tonic resolution.
An inverted pedal sustains the repeated tone in an upper voice rather than the bass, the held pitch sounding above the moving harmony instead of beneath it.
A bass ostinato, repeating a fixed pattern in the lowest voice, underpins variation forms such as the passacaglia, the recurring foundation supporting continuous elaboration above.
An ostinato establishes a rhythmic or harmonic groove against which syncopation and cross-rhythm in other voices acquire their disruptive effect.
A double pedal sustains two pitches at once, typically the tonic and dominant, the held interval forming a stable open frame beneath shifting harmony.
The pedal point relaxes strict voice-leading constraints, since the sustained tone is permitted to be dissonant against intervening chords without the usual preparation and resolution.
An ostinato pattern can itself migrate between voices or registers across a passage, the figure preserved intact while its placement in the texture changes.
A canon presents a single melody imitated strictly by one or more following voices. The leader states the line and each follower repeats it exactly after a fixed time interval.
A canon at the fifth has the following voice imitate the leader transposed by a perfect fifth. The transposition must be designed so the harmony remains correct against the leader.
A perpetual or circular canon, the round, ends where it begins, allowing endless repetition. Each voice rejoins the start of the melody as the others continue.
A mirror canon imitates the leader in inversion, every rising interval answered by a falling one. The follower traces an upside-down image of the leading melody.
A crab canon, or retrograde canon, sets the melody against its own backward statement, the two voices reading the same line in opposite directions simultaneously.
A mensuration canon imitates the leader at a different speed, the follower presenting the melody in augmentation or diminution while the leader proceeds at the original tempo.
Writing a canon requires that the melody work as counterpoint against its own delayed copy, every vertical interval between leader and follower satisfying the consonance rules.
A double canon runs two simultaneous canons at once, four voices arranged as two leader-follower pairs, the combined texture demanding careful contrapuntal planning.
The time interval of imitation, the delay between leader and follower entries, determines the harmonic relationships that arise and constrains how the melody must be composed.
A canon with a free voice adds an independent part that is not bound by the imitation, supplying harmonic support or contrapuntal variety alongside the strict canonic voices.
Rondo form alternates a recurring refrain with contrasting episodes. The refrain returns in the tonic each time, while the episodes explore other keys and contrasting material.
A five-part rondo follows the scheme refrain, first episode, refrain, second episode, refrain, the central episode often providing the strongest tonal and thematic contrast.

A seven-part rondo extends the alternation to refrain, episode, refrain, episode, refrain, episode, refrain, the first and third episodes sometimes related as in a sonata exposition and recapitulation.
The refrain of a rondo is typically a closed, tuneful theme ending with a clear cadence, its self-contained quality allowing it to recur intact without revision.
Episodes in a rondo modulate away from the tonic and may introduce developmental procedures, the contrast between stable refrain and mobile episode driving the form.
Transitions and retransitions link the refrain and episodes of a rondo, the retransition preparing each return of the refrain by leading the harmony back to the dominant of the tonic.
Sonata-rondo combines rondo's refrain logic with sonata's tonal plan, the first episode behaving as a secondary theme that returns transposed into the tonic in the final episode.
A coda often follows the last refrain of a rondo, extending the music past the structural cadence and gathering motivic fragments toward a decisive close.
The rondo's recurring refrain provides a familiar point of return, the listener's pleasure deriving partly from the anticipation and recognition of its repeated arrival.
Variation may enter a rondo when the refrain returns altered in figuration or orchestration, the recurrence freshened without disrupting the form's underlying alternation.

Tritone substitution replaces a dominant seventh chord with another dominant seventh whose root lies a tritone away. The two chords share the same third and seventh, the tritone that defines dominant function.
In a tritone substitution, the substituting dominant resolves down by a half step to the target, producing a smooth chromatic bass descent in place of the original descending-fifth motion.
The shared guide tones make the substitution work: the third of one dominant is the seventh of the other, so the essential tendency tones resolve identically in both spellings.
Applying tritone substitution to a two-five-one progression yields a chromatically descending bass line, the substitute dominant a half step above the target tonic.
A tritone substitute is often voiced with a sharp eleventh, the altered tension reflecting the chord's lydian-dominant character and reinforcing the substitution's bright color.
Tritone substitution can be applied to secondary dominants as well, the substitute chord tonicizing the same target through the equivalent tritone-related dominant.
The substitution preserves harmonic function while changing harmonic color, the same dominant resolution dressed in a chord rooted a tritone from the original.
Backdoor dominants are a related device, approaching the tonic from the flat-seventh dominant rather than the conventional fifth, another chromatic alternative to the standard resolution.
Tritone substitution exploits the symmetry of the tritone, which divides the octave in half, so the interval between the two substitutable dominant roots equals its own inversion.
