Chains of tritone-substituted dominants generate long chromatic descending sequences, each substitute resolving by half step into the next link of the progression.
The cadential six-four delays the dominant by placing a tonic triad in second inversion on a strong beat over the dominant scale degree in the bass.
Functionally the cadential six-four is a dominant embellishment, not a tonic chord. Its sixth and fourth above the bass are accented dissonances that resolve down to the fifth and third.
The two upper voices of a cadential six-four resolve by step: the sixth above the bass falls to the fifth, and the fourth falls to the third, while the bass holds the dominant.
The cadential six-four typically falls on a metrically strong beat, its accented dissonance carrying greater weight than the consonant dominant that follows it.
Analysts often label the cadential six-four with a dominant Roman numeral followed by six-four-to-five-three figures, emphasizing that the chord prolongs the dominant rather than the tonic.
Doubling in a cadential six-four follows the bass: the dominant scale degree is doubled, since it is the only stable tone while the sixth and fourth above are dissonant.
The cadential six-four heightens the sense of arrival at a cadence, the suspended dissonance increasing tension before the dominant resolves to the tonic.
Unlike the passing or pedal six-four, the cadential six-four is metrically accented and functionally dominant, distinguishing it sharply from those embellishing second-inversion chords.
In a concerto, the cadential six-four often precedes the soloist's cadenza, the orchestra arriving on the suspended dominant harmony that the cadenza will eventually resolve.
The cadential six-four can be prolonged across several beats, the dissonant upper voices held before resolving, stretching the moment of harmonic suspense at the cadence.
The medieval hexachord is a six-note pattern with the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, and la, containing a single half step between mi and fa.
Solmization assigned the hexachord syllables to scale steps for sight-singing, the mi-fa half step always marking the same interval regardless of where the hexachord began.
Three hexachords were recognized: the natural beginning on C, the hard beginning on G, and the soft beginning on F, the soft hexachord requiring a B-flat to keep the mi-fa half step.
Mutation allowed a singer to shift from one hexachord to another mid-melody, exchanging syllables on a shared pitch to extend the available range beyond a single six-note span.
The Guidonian hand mapped the hexachord syllables onto the joints of the hand, a mnemonic device that let singers locate pitches and practice sight-singing without notation.
Because the hexachord contains only one half step, the mi-fa pair, melodies were sung by tracking that half step, mutation supplying the rest of the gamut.
The complete medieval gamut overlapped the three hexachords across more than two octaves, the joined hexachords providing a continuous ladder of solmization syllables.
Movable-do solfege descends from hexachordal solmization, the syllables naming scale degrees relative to the tonic rather than fixed pitches.
Adding a seventh syllable for the leading tone later completed the diatonic octave, transforming the six-note hexachord system into the seven-note solfege still used today.
Solmization governed how musica ficta was applied, singers introducing unwritten accidentals to preserve the proper mi-fa half-step relationships of the hexachords.
Chromaticism introduces pitches outside the prevailing diatonic scale. Chromatic tones may decorate the surface as nonharmonic embellishments or alter chords to intensify harmonic function.
A chromatic passing tone fills a whole step with a half-step motion, the inserted chromatic pitch connecting two diatonic notes a tone apart by stepwise semitone motion.
Chromatic voice leading drives much of nineteenth-century harmony, individual voices moving by half step to connect chords that share few or no common tones.
A chromatic line, a melodic descent or ascent by successive half steps, can be harmonized in many ways, each chromatic pitch supporting a different passing or applied chord.
Chromatic third relations connect chords whose roots lie a major or minor third apart and that are not diatonically related, the shared common tone smoothing the colorful shift.
The chromatic scale, all twelve pitches, supplies the raw material; functional tonality organizes a subset of it diatonically while chromaticism reaches outside that subset for color and tension.
Omnibus progressions chain chromatic chords through wedge-shaped contrary motion, the outer voices spreading apart by half steps while inner voices hold or move minimally.
Excessive chromaticism can weaken a sense of key, the proliferation of altered tones obscuring the diatonic scale and pushing the music toward tonal ambiguity.
Chromatic mediants supply harmonic color without functional progression, the chords connected by a shared tone and a striking root motion by third rather than by fifth.
A chromaticized voice exchange swaps two voices through chromatic passing motion, the half-step inflections coloring a prolongation that would otherwise be purely diatonic.
Invertible counterpoint is written so that two voices can exchange registers, the upper becoming the lower and the lower becoming the upper, while remaining contrapuntally correct.
Counterpoint invertible at the octave shifts one voice by an octave so the parts swap position. Intervals transform predictably: a third becomes a sixth, a fifth becomes a fourth.
When inverting at the octave, the perfect fifth becomes a fourth and thus a dissonance, so fifths must be treated carefully in the original so the inversion remains consonant.
Counterpoint invertible at the twelfth allows the voices to exchange across a twelfth. The interval transformations differ, so the fifth remains consonant but other intervals shift accordingly.
Invertible counterpoint at the tenth supports the addition of parallel thirds or sixths, the inversion generating new consonant voices alongside the original two.
Triple counterpoint extends invertibility to three voices, all six possible vertical arrangements of the parts sounding correct, a demanding constraint on the original composition.
The countersubject of a fugue is typically composed in invertible counterpoint with the subject so that subject and countersubject can sound in either vertical order during the piece.
Designing invertible counterpoint requires anticipating which intervals will become dissonant after inversion and treating those intervals as dissonances even in the original arrangement.
Double counterpoint, the invertibility of two voices, is the most common form, the term double distinguishing it from triple and quadruple invertible textures.
Invertible counterpoint enriches a contrapuntal work by allowing the same combination of lines to be reused in varied registral arrangements without composing new material.
Chorale harmonization sets a given melody in four parts, the tune usually in the soprano and the bass, tenor, and alto supplying harmony that supports it phrase by phrase.
Each phrase of a chorale ends with a cadence, the harmonization choosing authentic, half, or plagal cadences to articulate the melody's structure and punctuate its line.
Harmonizing a chorale begins by choosing chords for the cadence points, then filling in the intervening melody notes with progressions that connect those structural goals smoothly.
The bass line of a chorale harmonization should be melodically shapely in its own right, providing a strong contrapuntal counterpart to the soprano while grounding the harmony.
Passing tones, neighbor tones, and suspensions enliven the inner voices of a chorale, the embellishments adding rhythmic interest without disturbing the underlying harmonic framework.
A fermata in a chorale marks the end of a phrase, the harmonization supplying a cadence at each fermata to give the melody its periodic resting points.
Voice leading governs every chord connection in a chorale harmonization, common tones held, leading tones resolved, and parallel perfect intervals scrupulously avoided.
The same chorale melody can be harmonized in many ways, the choice of chords and cadences reflecting the harmonizer's interpretation of the tune's phrase structure.
A walking bass in a chorale harmonization moves in steady note values, often filling the spaces between structural bass notes with stepwise passing motion.
Reharmonization revisits a familiar chorale melody with fresh chords, the new harmony recasting the same tune in a different harmonic light while preserving the soprano line.
Symmetrical scales divide the octave into equal or repeating interval segments. Their internal symmetry limits the number of distinct transpositions before the pattern repeats itself.
The whole-tone scale, built entirely of whole steps, has only two distinct transpositions, since shifting it by a whole tone reproduces the same six-note collection.
The octatonic scale alternates half and whole steps and yields just three transpositions, the minor-third symmetry of the pattern collapsing the twelve possible starting points into three.
Messiaen catalogued the modes of limited transposition, scales whose symmetrical interval structure permits fewer than twelve distinct transpositions before the pitch content recurs.
The augmented scale, alternating minor thirds and half steps, divides the octave symmetrically into three equal major-third spans, repeating after a transposition of a major third.
Symmetrical scales obscure a tonal center because their even interval structure lacks the asymmetry that, in the diatonic scale, singles out one pitch as tonic.
The octatonic collection contains multiple diminished seventh chords and dominant seventh chords, its symmetry supplying a rich harmonic vocabulary favored in colorful, nonfunctional writing.
Transposing a symmetrical scale by its interval of symmetry leaves the collection unchanged, the property that defines the limited-transposition class to which the scale belongs.
Symmetrical divisions of the octave underlie much chromatic harmony, the equal partitions producing chord relationships, such as the chromatic mediant cycle, that bypass functional tonality.
The chromatic scale itself is the most symmetrical collection, dividing the octave into twelve equal half steps and admitting only a single transposition since every shift reproduces it.
Cadential evasion thwarts an expected resolution at the last moment, the dominant failing to reach the anticipated tonic and the music continuing past the would-be ending.
An elided cadence overlaps the end of one phrase with the beginning of the next, the tonic that resolves one phrase simultaneously launching the following phrase.
Evading a cadence by suddenly changing register, dynamics, or harmony delays closure and propels the music forward, the postponed resolution heightening anticipation.
A deceptive cadence is one form of evasion, the dominant resolving to the submediant instead of the tonic, the false resolution extending the phrase toward a later true cadence.
The one-more-time technique repeats the approach to a cadence after an evasion, the music backing up to retry the resolution and often expanding the phrase in the process.
Phrase elision compresses musical time by suppressing the silence or repose that would normally separate two phrases, the units interlocking at a shared structural pitch.
An abandoned cadence breaks off before the resolving chord arrives, the dominant left hanging as the music veers into new material without completing the expected progression.
Evaded and elided cadences sustain forward momentum across what would otherwise be sectional boundaries, knitting phrases into a continuous, goal-directed harmonic flow.
A cadence may be reinterpreted: the chord that ends one phrase becomes a pivot beginning a modulation, the closural arrival reassigned a new function in the following passage.
The strongest structural cadence of a movement is often reserved for the final phrase, earlier evasions and elisions deferring full closure until the concluding resolution.
